    AI Overview
    The "No Tax on Tips" policy, implemented via the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), allows eligible workers in over 70 tipped occupations to deduct up to $25,000 in voluntarily received cash tips from their federal income taxes from 2025–2028. The deduction, which excludes automatic gratuities, applies to employees in food service, hospitality, and personal services who report their tips. 
    Key Details of the "No Tax on Tips" Provision 
    • Eligibility: Workers must be in a "customarily tipped" occupation, such as restaurant servers, bartenders, hairdressers, valets, and taxi drivers.
    • Qualified Tips: Only voluntary cash tips (including credit card tips) qualify. Automatic service charges for large parties are not included
      .
    • Deduction Limit: Up to
      per tax year in tips can be deducted, with the benefit phasing out for individuals with a modified adjusted gross income over
      (
       for joint filers).
    • Reporting Requirement: Tips must be reported to the employer for payroll tax purposes to qualify for the exemption.
    • Income Threshold: Individuals earning less than the standard deduction—
       for individuals or
      for married couples in 2025—will not see a benefit as they already owe no federal income tax.       
    Impact on Workers 
    • Eligible Occupations: The IRS has identified over 70 occupations in sectors such as food/beverage, hospitality, personal services, and entertainment that qualify for the deduction.
    • Effective Period: The tax deduction for tips is valid for the 2025 through 2028 tax years.
    • State-Level Action: Several states, including Arizona, California, Georgia, and others, have proposed their own versions of "no tax on tips" legislation, as shown on EPI.org. 
    Limitations 
    • The policy does not exempt tips from Social Security or Medicare taxes, only federal income tax.
    • It does not apply to automatic gratuities, which are treated as taxable wages.
    • The deduction is only applicable if the tips are officially reported, which may impact workers who rely on unreported cash tips. 
    For more specific information on how to file your taxes under this new rule, refer to the official IRS newsroom.
